source.title: TruthfulQA: Measuring How Models Mimic Human Falsehoods
source.authors: Stephanie C. Lin; Jacob Hilton; Owain Evans

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some figures have garbled OCR, but the relevant truthfulness values are also reported in a table and the text.
record.tranche_reason: It measures downstream benchmark performance across model sizes, but tests truthfulness rather than held-out cross-entropy or the original scaling-law method.
record.gate_note: The paper tests truthfulness on a question-answering benchmark across model sizes and reports matched-control results. It does not measure held-out loss, fit power laws, test extrapolation from smaller runs, find compute-optimal allocations, or compare architecture shapes. Scaling laws are cited as motivation, not tested. Results from newer models in Appendix B.3 are external evaluations and are not recorded as this study's results.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates existing GPT-3, GPT-Neo/J, GPT-2 and UnifiedQA checkpoints of several sizes on a downstream QA benchmark. It reports truthfulness falling with model size ("inverse scaling"), which bears directly on V6's claim that downstream performance improves with scale. The benchmark was built adversarially, and the result runs against V6, so T5 fits better than T2. It measures no loss, fits no power laws, and tests nothing on V1–V5 or V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors find that larger models in each family are generally less truthful but more informative on TruthfulQA, while improving on matched controls. They attribute this to imitative falsehoods learned from the training distribution. They conclude scaling alone is less promising than fine-tuning with objectives other than imitating web text, possibly combined with prompting.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates zero-shot generated answers on a truthfulness benchmark across existing model sizes, using human judgments; it does not measure pretraining loss or fit scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: Truthfulness varies substantially with prompt for GPT-3 175B: the reported % True values range from 12.5% with the harmful prompt to 58.1% with the helpful prompt. The authors state that different prompts significantly affect truthfulness.
record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, 2021
record.problems: The benchmark was deliberately designed to elicit falsehoods and may exploit some non-imitative weaknesses. The authors note that semantic weaknesses cannot be fully ruled out. The main size comparisons report no uncertainty values in the table; human evaluation also involves a single participant as the human baseline.
record.rows_left_out: None. The included rows are below the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss measured; no power-law fit.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
No architecture-shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
No other modalities or training regimes studied as scaling laws.
Downstream performance is not related to pretraining loss. No functional fit or predictability test: only a direction of change across 2–4 sizes per family is reported.
No fitting choices or exponents examined.

missing.what: Informativeness (% Info) rises with size in all families (GPT-3 72.7→97.6%; GPT-Neo/J 54.3→90.0%; GPT-2 68.8→89.8%; UnifiedQA 49.2→64.5%). This is a capability measure improving with scale alongside falling truthfulness.

Truth score on the unfiltered questions only, which were not adversarially filtered against GPT-3 175B, still declines with size (GPT-3 0.378→0.284; GPT-Neo/J 0.384→0.287). This addresses the worry that the filtering targeted the largest model.
missing.locator: Table 4 (Truth score unf.); Appendix B.4, Figure 12

missing.what: The inverse trend is replicated under the GPT-judge metric, at temperature 1, and on paraphrased questions.
missing.locator: Table 4 (%True GPT-judge); Appendix B.8, Figure 19; Appendix B.9, Figure 20

record.verdict_notes: Several features of the study constrain how far the V6 challenge generalises. TruthfulQA was adversarially built: 437 of 817 questions were filtered against GPT-3-175B. The authors use the Neo/J consistency, unfiltered subset, controls and paraphrases to argue the inverse trend reflects imitative falsehoods rather than adversarial artefacts. Each family has only 2–4 sizes, with no uncertainty reported for the main comparisons. Appendix B.3 reports external evaluations (Anthropic, Gopher, InstructGPT) showing a "return to positive scaling" at large sizes on multiple-choice. Without context distillation, Anthropic's model shows inverse scaling. These are external results and are not counted here, but researchers comparing studies should note them. Rows r1, r10, r14 and r16 are the smallest models in each family and serve as baselines (cannot_determine is fine). The reader's separate limits_scope label for r12/r19 was dropped: those upticks sit inside overall declining trends and are folded into the challenges label.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss and power-law relations in parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of larger-run losses from power laws fitted on small runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation at fixed compute.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Power-law scaling in other modalities or training regimes.
The study evaluates truthfulness on one zero-shot question-answering benchmark; it does not test general downstream-task performance or relate performance to pretraining loss.
Dependence of loss-law exponents or compute-optimal splits on setup and fitting choices.

relationships.condition: TruthfulQA questions (generation, human-judged % true; multiple-choice), across GPT-3, GPT-Neo/J, GPT-2 and UnifiedQA families
relationships.reason: Truthfulness falls with size in every family: GPT-3 37.0→20.4%, GPT-Neo/J 43.6→26.8%, GPT-2 35.4→29.3%, UnifiedQA 58.0→54.0%. Multiple-choice is also worse at larger sizes. Small upticks at r12 and r19 do not alter the trend (r2-r4, r11-r13, r15, r17-r20, r22).
relationships.display_finding: Generation truthfulness fell from 37.0% to 20.4% for GPT-3, 43.6% to 26.8% for GPT-Neo/J, 35.4% to 29.3% for GPT-2 and 58.0% to 54.0% for UnifiedQA; multiple-choice performance also worsened with size despite small local upticks.
